The contradictory data suggests that people as a whole disagree with one another and that individuals change their stance depending on the moral issue. A more difficult question: Is morality actually objective or subjective? The majority of living philosophers are moral realists, meaning that they believe that there are mind-independent, objective moral truths. The history of philosophy is littered with countless attempts to objectively ground morality. Objective accounts can be grouped under one of these broad views:

  1. Moral non-naturalism: objective, mind-independent moral facts exist non-naturally (but not supernaturally) in a similar way as mathematical numbers exist
  2. Moral naturalism: objective, mind-independent moral facts exist, but they are reducible to natural facts about what would contribute to overall human-flourishing
  3. Moral constructivism: moral facts are not mind-independent, but they are objective in the same way as logical laws

Personally, I believe that there are no objective moral truths. But I also believe that there are not any subjective moral truths. While there are certainly facts about whether cultures or individuals believe certain things are right or wrong, those beliefs cannot ground what I believe is essential to morality: objective prescriptivity. Take the claim: "It is morally wrong for websites to censor content." Do we simply mean that censorship would not be in the best interest of most people? I think we mean something stronger that is captured by the idea of objective prescriptivity: regardless of what the majority of people believe, there are facts about what we should do, and censoring content is something that should not be done. This means that all moral facts would have to be objective, and we return to the problem of grounding described above.

How do we get out of this problem? The position that I hold is called moral error theory, or moral nihilism. I believe that, in order for a moral claim to be true, there has to be an objective moral fact. But I do not think any such moral facts exist. This position is extremely unpopular in both the general public and philosophy, but it has been growing in popularity since Mackie published in 1977. If you are more interested, I would recommend reading his essay The Subjectivity of Values. That essay is mandatory reading for metaethics students, because it outlines the central arguments for moral error theory. There are numerous questions that one might have about this position (feel free to ask me below), but I just want to say one last thing. Being a moral nihilist does not mean you care any less about the well-being of others. It simply means that those are our subjective values. There is no fact of the matter about what is right or wrong, but it does not make us any less willing to fight, and even die, to protect the well-being of others.

tl;dr Morality requires objective values, but no such objective values exist.

Hello,

I'm currently working on a webservice (a personal project). While figuring out which features I want to have from the start, and features which I don't want at all to have for now, I got thinking about the Like feature of many many webservices. While Facebook is what you immediately think nowadays whenever you hear "Like", it's by far not the only one. We're here on voat, where a upvoted submission rises to the top. And so on.

I have an issue with it.

First, let's say you're in a rate-my-photo group. You post a well-done photo. What ends up happening? Your post get's "liked" (or upvoated) some times, and then it vanishes in the endless content stream of big social media sites. What happens if you post something bad? That post get's comment after comment, actual discussions ensue. That's great. But it also let's some service think that it's good content and "stays on top" for a long period of time.

Second, the psychological effect. You posted something. You put a lot of effort into that post.

What do you see?

  • A like: Nothing!
  • 56 likes: A number
  • A comment saying "Wow, great photo!": Someone who just appreciated your efforts. A human response.

What do you think? What would be a good system from a content creators perspective?
Let's discuss the "Like" feature of oh so many internet services

While comments certainly mean much more than likes or upvoats, a lot of people simply don't want to take the time and effort to type out a comment. So I think a "like" feature is important to let users know that even though others aren't saying anything with words, they appreciate their content.

Mh, the time factor may be an obstacle - Sadly. I can't come up with a solution to it though really. I have nothing against a Like feature itself. It's fine, I just don't like the implications. Other services, like DeviantArt for instance, show a "Write a comment too!" sign above the favorite button there.

Two obversations: Favorites are less often given by people it seems. Second, that note never got me to comment..

I think the number of comments is most interesting, up to a certain point where so many comments are made, that a new viewer will not read all of them or feel the need to contribute to an extensive discussion.

As it is very hard to determine that sweet spot, I think the "likes" system was easier to implement for most sites.

To remedy this and use the comments as a guideline, I'd couple it with an indicator of how recent the content and discussion actually is. You'd have to think up an algorithm for that, but it could be something like this:

There are 50 comments to an item

The last 10% of comments are made within the last 72 hours

The last 20% of comments are made within the last 96 hours

72/5=14.4

96/10=9.6

14.4+9.6=24 <- this is the rating you give the specific item

The rating decides the prominence and order of items on the website.

This rating would take both news value and content value in to account, and would, imho, be a better system than just likes or comments.

Of course you could extend this to incorporate other mechanisms, like how many times has an item been added to favorites or saves, and give a rating to that too.

Anyway, that's my 2 cents.
